item.title: The Entry-Level Squeeze: Why Recent Grads Are Struggling to Land a First Job as Employers Lean on AI
item.body:
For decades, a college degree worked like a dependable ticket into the workforce. Graduate in May, start a job by fall. That pattern is looking less certain. Over the past couple of years, unemployment among recent college graduates has climbed above the overall national rate, a reversal of the long-standing norm in which degree holders fared better than the average worker. At the same time, employers are openly rethinking what a "junior" role should look like as artificial intelligence tools take over many routine tasks.

This article walks through what the data suggests, which fields appear most exposed, and what it could mean for the next generation of workers. It is a general overview, not career or financial advice.

## What the Numbers Show

Federal Reserve Bank of New York research and U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data have both pointed to the same trend: young, college-educated workers are having a harder time finding work than in the recent past. In several recent readings, the unemployment rate for recent graduates (typically ages 22 to 27) has been higher than the rate for all workers. Historically, that gap ran the other way.

A few details are worth keeping in mind:

- **The gap is relative, not catastrophic.** Most recent graduates do find work. But the time it takes, and the share who end up in jobs that do not require a degree, have both drawn attention.
- **Underemployment matters too.** Many graduates take roles below their qualifications while they keep searching, which headline unemployment figures do not capture.
- **Several forces overlap.** Higher interest rates, cautious corporate hiring, a large number of graduates, and post-pandemic adjustments have all played a part. AI is one factor among several, and economists disagree about how large its role is so far.

## Why Junior Roles Are Under Pressure

Entry-level jobs have traditionally served two purposes: getting basic work done and training the next generation of experienced staff. Much of that basic work consists of tasks such as drafting summaries, cleaning up data, writing first-pass code, researching background material, and preparing routine reports.

Those are the kinds of tasks that modern AI tools handle reasonably well. Some hiring managers say they can now accomplish with a smaller team, or with a few experienced people using AI assistants, what once required a larger group that included several new hires. Others say they are simply being more selective, hiring fewer juniors and expecting those they do hire to arrive with stronger practical skills.

There is a caveat. Surveys of employers show mixed intentions, and some companies say they are still hiring beginners, or even expanding programs for them. It is also hard to separate AI-driven change from the ordinary hiring cycle, in which companies pull back when the economy looks uncertain.

## Which Fields Appear Hardest Hit

Researchers and labor analysts have noted that exposure varies widely by field.

- **Software and tech support.** Computer science graduates, once seen as nearly guaranteed a strong job market, have faced a tougher environment as companies trimmed headcount and AI coding assistants became common.
- **Marketing, content and communications.** Entry-level writing, editing and basic design work are areas where generative tools are widely used.
- **Administrative and customer support roles.** Routine inquiries and scheduling are increasingly automated.
- **Finance and accounting support.** Data entry, reconciliation and first-pass analysis are being streamlined.
- **Paralegal and research work.** Document review and summarization are common AI use cases.

By contrast, fields that rely on hands-on, in-person or credential-gated work, such as nursing and other healthcare roles, skilled trades, and education, have generally seen steadier demand. That does not mean they are risk-free, but the pressure looks different.

## The Longer-Term Worry: A Broken Ladder

The biggest concern among economists is not only whether this year's graduates find jobs. It is what happens if fewer entry-level positions exist over several years. Experienced professionals are developed by doing junior work first. If that rung of the ladder shrinks, companies may face a shortage of mid-level talent later on, and workers may find it harder to build the experience that employers want.

Some employers are already experimenting with responses, such as apprenticeships, rotational programs, and redesigned junior roles that focus on judgment, client contact and supervising AI output rather than producing every first draft by hand.

## What Graduates Can Do

There is no guaranteed formula, but career counselors and labor experts commonly suggest several practical steps:

1. **Build demonstrable skills.** Internships, co-ops, freelance projects and portfolios give employers evidence beyond a transcript.
2. **Learn to work with AI tools.** Showing that you can use them well, check their output and catch their errors is increasingly seen as a baseline expectation.
3. **Develop human-centered strengths.** Communication, collaboration, problem framing and persuasion remain hard to automate.
4. **Widen the search.** Smaller firms, public-sector roles, nonprofits and industries outside your major may be more open to beginners.
5. **Use your network.** Referrals still account for a meaningful share of hires, especially when applicant volumes are high.
6. **Stay flexible.** A first job rarely defines an entire career, and many people move across fields within a few years.

## What Policymakers and Schools Are Weighing

Universities are reviewing how well their programs match employer needs, and many are adding AI literacy to their curricula. Policymakers and workforce groups are discussing support for apprenticeships, retraining programs and clearer labor-market data so students can make better-informed choices. Whether those efforts will keep pace with the technology remains an open question.

## Bottom Line

The data points to a genuinely harder market for new graduates than they have seen in years, with AI changing how employers think about beginner roles. Yet the picture is still developing. Economists caution against drawing sweeping conclusions from a few years of numbers, and the hiring cycle could shift again. For now, the most reliable advice is to build real-world experience, stay adaptable, and treat AI as a tool to master rather than only a threat.

*This article is for general informational purposes only and does not constitute career, financial or investment advice. Figures and trends change over time; consult the latest releases from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for current data.*
